screens.title: Deploying with Hardhat
screens.subtitle: From local networks to Sepolia and Mainnet — secure builds, deployment scripts, and post-deploy interactions

narration.text: In this chapter we take a practical, secure path to deploying smart contracts with Hardhat. You will learn how to configure the project, wire up networks using RPC endpoints, and keep private keys and A P I keys out of source control. We’ll step through real deployment scripts written with ethers. js, including a live-style walkthrough of deploying and interacting with a Greeter contract and an ERC‑20 token on Sepolia. You’ll also learn common error messages you will encounter, why they happen, and how to fix them — everything from insufficient funds to constructor revert conditions and chain ID mismatch. Finally, we’ll show how Hardhat tasks can automate post‑deployment actions like updating a greeting without redeploying. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to prepare a secure hardhat. config. js, execute deployment scripts against a chosen network, and verify addresses on a block explorer. Think of this as a deployment checklist: secure secrets, choose the right RPC, fund your deployer, run the script, and verify the result. Which part of the deployment workflow do you expect will require the most attention in your project?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Practical deployment is as important as contract design: configuration, secure keys, and correct network settings prevent lost funds and failed transactions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map directly to practical skills you will use when deploying smart contracts with Hardhat. First, you will learn how to configure a Hardhat project to target local networks and public testnets or Mainnet by editing the hardhat. config. js file and setting RPC endpoints. This matters because the correct network settings control signing and gas parameters. Second, you will write and run deployment scripts using ethers. js. You’ll practice getting a ContractFactory, calling deploy, and waiting for confirmations so that your code runs reliably. Third, you will manage private keys and A P I keys securely using environment variables and a. env file excluded from version control; this prevents accidental exposure of secrets. Finally, you will diagnose and resolve common deployment errors that stop transactions from being mined or from succeeding. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you can confirm competency by actually deploying a simple contract to Sepolia and interacting with it programmatically. These objectives prepare you to move from development to safe, reproducible deployments.

keyIdea.title: Skills aligned to practice
keyIdea.text: Configuration, scripting, secret management, and troubleshooting are the core competencies needed for reliable contract deployment.

screens.title: How these objectives translate to practice
screens.subtitle: A closer look at verification milestones and practical checks

narration.text: Beyond simply reading configuration files, you will practice a short checklist that verifies each deployment step. For configuration, that means confirming your RPC URL responds and that the chain ID matches the intended network. For scripts, it means your deployment script compiles the contract, sends the transaction, and waits for one or more confirmations. For secrets, it means your PRIVATE_KEY is only referenced through process. env and the. env file is listed in. gitignore. For diagnostics, you will reproduce and interpret common console errors: insufficient funds, revert messages from constructor logic, long pending transactions, and chain ID mismatches. Each of these checks maps to an action you can perform immediately — query your account balance, simulate a constructor call locally, increase gas settings, or cross-check the chain ID. Practically, the milestone for this chapter is to deploy a small ERC‑20 on Sepolia, confirm the minted balance, and verify the contract address on a block explorer. This hands-on approach teaches not just what to change, but how to verify that your change worked.

keyIdea.text: A reproducible checklist — confirm RPC, fund accounts, run scripts, and verify addresses — turns deployment into a predictable operation.

screens.title: What is Hardhat and why use it?
screens.subtitle: A development environment, local network, and plugin system tailored for Ethereum

narration.text: Hardhat is a development environment that brings compilation, testing, scripting, and a local Ethereum network together in one toolset. The local Hardhat Network enables rapid iteration: you can compile contracts and run transactions instantly without waiting on public networks. Hardhat’s extensible plugin system adds capabilities such as Ethers. js integration, gas reporting, and Etherscan verification that align with deployment workflows. The practical reason to use Hardhat is reproducibility — a single hardhat. config. js file records compiler versions, network endpoints, and plugin settings so builds and deployments behave consistently across machines and CI. For example, when you set the Solidity version and the compiler settings in the configuration, compiled artifacts stay consistent so the deployed bytecode is predictable. A common misconception is that Hardhat replaces learning ethers. js or the Ethereum protocol; it does not. Instead, Hardhat provides the scaffolding and developer ergonomics to use ethers. js effectively and to script deployment logic that interacts with real networks. Takeaway: Hardhat speeds development, enforces reproducible builds, and integrates the libraries and plugins you need for secure, repeatable deployments. What is Hardhat and why use it? means hardhat bundles a local chain, task runner, and plugin ecosystem to simplify building, testing, and deploying contracts.. In practical terms, a development environment, local network, and plugin system tailored for ethereum. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Configuring hardhat.config.js for networks
screens.subtitle: Record compiler, plugin, and network settings for reproducible deployments

narration.text: The hardhat. config. js file is the central record for how your project is compiled and deployed. It sets the Solidity compiler version, plugin options like the toolbox and gas reporter, and — crucially — network configurations that include RPC URLs, accounts, and chain IDs. When you deploy to public networks such as Sepolia or Mainnet you typically specify an RPC URL from a provider and an account private key read from environment variables. This ensures the sensitive key is never in source control. A common pattern is to require dotenv at the top of the config, read process. env. SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and process. env. PRIVATE_KEY, and then expose them in the networks section. A misconception is that adding an RPC URL is enough; in practice you also must supply the account array and correct chainId so signing and transaction validation succeed. As an example of practice, include a gas reporter configuration and an etherscan A P I key for verification. After editing the config, validate it by running a local compile and a simple deployment against hardhat or Sepolia. The immediate payoff is predictable bytecode and a documented deployment target.

keyIdea.title: Config principle
keyIdea.text: hardhat.config.js captures the build and network recipe so deployments are repeatable and auditable.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Configuring hardhat.config.js
Code Walkthrough

Example hardhat.config.js

// hardhat.config.js
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox");
require("dotenv").config();

const SEPOLIA_RPC_URL = process.env.SEPOLIA_RPC_URL || "https://eth-sepolia.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_ALCHEMY_API_KEY";
const MAINNET_RPC_URL = process.env.MAINNET_RPC_URL || "https://eth-mainnet.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_ALCHEMY_API_KEY";
const PRIVATE_KEY = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY;

module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.20",
  networks: {
    hardhat: {},
    sepolia: {
      url: SEPOLIA_RPC_URL,
      accounts: PRIVATE_KEY !== undefined ? [PRIVATE_KEY] : [],
      chainId: 11155111,
    },
    mainnet: {
      url: MAINNET_RPC_URL,
      accounts: PRIVATE_KEY !== undefined ? [PRIVATE_KEY] : [],
      chainId: 1,
    },
  },
  etherscan: { apiKey: process.env.ETHERSCAN_API_KEY },
};
Explanation & Checklist
  • Always load secrets with dotenv and process.env to avoid committing keys.
  • Provide accounts as an array when PRIVATE_KEY exists; otherwise keep blank for local testing.
  • Match chainId to the network to avoid signing errors at send time.
  • Include plugins like etherscan and gasReporter if you intend to verify or measure gas.
Concrete example
If you set SEPOLIA_RPC_URL to your Alchemy endpoint and place your deployer PRIVATE_KEY in .env, running a deploy with --network sepolia will sign with that key and send the transaction to Sepolia.
Key Takeaway

Validate your config by compiling and running a short deploy to confirm network connectivity and signing behavior.

screens.title: Managing private keys and API keys securely
screens.subtitle: Use environment variables and .env files; never hardcode secrets

narration.text: Security in deployment starts with secrets management. Hardcoding private keys or A P I keys in your repository is a common and costly mistake because public repositories are indexed and can lead to irreversible key compromise. Instead, the recommended pattern is to store sensitive values in a. env file at your project root and load them using the dotenv package. Place. env in. gitignore so it never reaches version control. Then reference secrets through process. env variables in hardhat. config. js and scripts. When you run deployment scripts in CI, inject environment variables securely via the CI provider rather than committing a. env file. For local testing, keep a separate test key with minimal funds to limit risk. Another common misconception is that environment variables are automatically secure; they are convenient but depend on the host environment. Always treat any environment variable with the same care as a key in a password manager. A quick practical check is to run git status to confirm. env is untracked and to print the deployer address from the script rather than the private key. These steps reduce the chance of leaked credentials and make deployment safer in team and CI settings.

keyIdea.title: Security rule
keyIdea.text: Never commit secrets; use .env, dotenv, and secure CI injects to keep keys out of source control.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Manage secrets
Definition & Best Practice
Store keys in a local .env file and load them with dotenv. Add .env to .gitignore and use CI environment variables for automation.
Example .env
SEPOLIA_RPC_URL="https://eth-sepolia.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_ALCHEMY_API_KEY"
PRIVATE_KEY="YOUR_DEPLOYER_PRIVATE_KEY_HERE"
ETHERSCAN_API_KEY="YOUR_ETHERSCAN_API_KEY_HERE"
  • Use separate keys for local testing vs production.
  • Limit the balance of test keys to reduce risk if leaked.
  • Rotate keys if exposure is suspected.
Practical checks
  1. Run git status to ensure .env is not tracked.
  2. Print deployer address, never the private key, in deployment logs.
  3. Use CI secret injection for automated runs, not committed files.
Common Mistake

Hardcoding keys in scripts or config files. If you find a key in history, rotate immediately.

screens.title: Writing and running a deployment script with ethers.js
screens.subtitle: Deploy, wait for confirmation, and interact post-deployment

narration.text: Deployment scripts are the bridge between your compiled artifacts and the live blockchain. Using the ethers. js integration that comes with Hardhat, you typically get a ContractFactory for your contract, call deploy with the constructor arguments, and then await deployed. This forces compilation if needed and sends a signed transaction from your configured signer. After the transaction is mined, you can call public view functions to confirm on‑chain state and even send subsequent transactions to modify state. A concrete example is a Greeter contract: your script prints the deployer address and balance, deploys Greeter with an initial greeting string, waits for it to be deployed, and then calls greet and setGreeting while waiting for the confirmation for the second transaction. A common misconception is that. deploy() returns a fully confirmed contract immediately. In practice you get a Contract instance that represents the deployment transaction; calling await contract. deployed() ensures the transaction is mined. Always log the deployed address and consider waiting for an extra confirmation in production to reduce the chance of reorgs. These practices make deployments observable and auditable.

keyIdea.title: Deployment flow
keyIdea.text: Get a ContractFactory, call deploy, await deployment, then interact and wait for tx confirmations.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Deployment Script
Script example
// scripts/deployGreeter.js
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();
  console.log("Deploying contracts with the account:", deployer.address);
  console.log("Account balance:", (await deployer.getBalance()).toString());

  const Greeter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Greeter");
  console.log("Deploying Greeter...");
  const greeter = await Greeter.deploy("Hello, Cohortia!");

  await greeter.deployed();
  console.log("Greeter deployed to:", greeter.address);

  let currentGreeting = await greeter.greet();
  console.log("Current greeting:", currentGreeting);

  const tx = await greeter.setGreeting("Welcome to Web3 Development!");
  await tx.wait();
  console.log("Greeting updated!");
}

main().catch((error) => { console.error(error); process.exit(1); });
Key steps explained
  • Get the deployer signer via ethers.getSigners() to sign transactions.
  • Use getContractFactory to obtain an object that can deploy new instances.
  • Call deploy with constructor args and await deployed for mining.
  • Interact post-deploy and wait for transaction confirmations with tx.wait().
Scenario
Deploy Greeter to Sepolia, call greet and update it, and confirm the updated state is visible on-chain by reading the getter.
Key Takeaway

Always wait for transactions to be mined before relying on on-chain state changes.

screens.title: Running scripts on specific networks
screens.subtitle: How to invoke Hardhat scripts with the --network flag and what to verify before running

narration.text: Running a deployment on a chosen network uses the --network flag to direct Hardhat to the correct RPC and signer settings defined in hardhat. config. js. The typical command is npx hardhat run scripts/deployGreeter. js --network sepolia. Before running this, verify three things: your SEPOLIA_RPC_URL responds, your PRIVATE_KEY is loaded and corresponds to an address with sufficient balance, and the chainId in your config matches the network. If any of these are off you will see errors such as insufficient funds or chainId mismatch during signing. A concrete pre-run checklist: 1) curl or use eth_chainId on the endpoint to ensure the provider is reachable; 2) print the deployer address and its balance from the script; 3) ensure the account has test ETH from a faucet for Sepolia. For CI or automated runs, inject the environment variables in the runner and avoid committing secrets. A common misconception is that local Hardhat settings are enough for public networks; they are not — you must explicitly provide the public RPC and the appropriate account. After a successful run, copy the logged contract address for verification on block explorers.

keyIdea.title: Execution checklist
keyIdea.text: Confirm RPC, fund your deployer, and provide the network flag so Hardhat routes the script to the intended chain.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Running scripts
Process

Run a script on Sepolia

# Run deployment on Sepolia
npx hardhat run scripts/deployGreeter.js --network sepolia
Pre-run checks
  • Ensure SEPOLIA_RPC_URL is reachable and returns a chain ID.
  • Confirm deployer address from PRIVATE_KEY has test ETH.
  • Double-check chainId and account format in config.
Terminal output example
Deploying contracts with the account: 0xYourAddress
Account balance: 1000000000000000000
Greeter deployed to: 0xDeployedAddress
Post-run action
Copy the deployed address and verify it on the block explorer or via etherscan plugin when available.
Key Takeaway

The --network flag selects the runtime target; ensure your environment and account are ready before running.

screens.title: Common deployment errors and how to fix them
screens.subtitle: Insufficient funds, revert messages, pending transactions, and chainId mismatches

narration.text: Deployments can fail for a handful of recurring reasons. The first is insufficient funds: the deployer account simply lacks the ETH to pay for gas. The fix is straightforward — obtain test ETH from a faucet for testnets or transfer funds on Mainnet. Second, constructor revert or missing revert data indicates a problem in constructor logic or constructor arguments; double-check inputs and run the constructor locally to simulate the failure. Third, transactions not mined within the expected time happen when gas price is set too low or the RPC provider is unreliable. You can increase gasPrice or the EIP-1559 fields maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas in the transaction options or the Hardhat config. Fourth, an incorrect chainId in the config leads to signing errors because the signer uses the wrong network context; verify the chainId value matches the target network. A common misconception is to treat these errors as mysterious; they are diagnostic clues. Read the error, check account balance, simulate the constructor call locally, and adjust gas settings or provider accordingly. A clear diagnostic strategy saves time: confirm balance, check constructor args, and validate chain IDs.

keyIdea.title: Diagnostics pattern
keyIdea.text: Treat error messages as direct signals: check balance, constructor inputs, gas parameters, and chain IDs in that order.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Common Errors
Error: insufficient funds
Cause: Deployer address lacks ETH. Fix: Fund from a faucet or transfer test ETH, then retry.
Error: constructor revert
Cause: Constructor logic failed or wrong args. Fix: Verify parameters and run local tests to replicate the failure.
Error: tx not mined within X seconds
Cause: Low gas price or provider issue. Fix: Increase gasPrice or EIP-1559 fields or switch provider.
Error: incorrect chainId
Cause: chainId in config mismatches network. Fix: Set chainId to the network's ID in hardhat.config.js.
Quick diagnostic checklist
  • Check deployer balance.
  • Simulate constructor locally with hardhat or a unit test.
  • Verify RPC provider responsiveness and gas settings.
  • Confirm chainId and account configuration.
Common misconception
Treating timeouts as random: usually they indicate provider issues or insufficient gas — not an inscrutable network error.
Key Takeaway

Follow the diagnostic pattern: balance, constructor, gas/provider, chainId — in that order — to quickly resolve deployment failures.

screens.title: Understanding gas settings and the gas reporter
screens.subtitle: Estimate costs, configure gas parameters, and use the gas reporter plugin

narration.text: Gas is the unit that measures computation cost on Ethereum, and gas settings determine whether your transaction is accepted and included in a block. For EIP-1559 style networks you can set maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas, while legacy networks may use gasPrice. If you set these values too low a transaction may remain pending and ultimately time out. When deploying to Mainnet you must estimate gas carefully to avoid overspending unexpectedly. Hardhat supports a gas reporter plugin that prints estimated costs in your test runs and can be enabled or disabled via environment variables. A pragmatic workflow is to run tests with the gas reporter enabled to get an idea of expected deployment costs, then set conservative fee values for live runs or rely on provider-recommended fees. A misconception is that gas estimation always matches real-world fees; network volatility and block congestion alter actual costs, so add margins for production deployments. Use the gas reporter as a planning tool and handle fees dynamically when possible to balance cost and speed. Understanding gas settings and the gas reporter means estimate in tests with the gas reporter, then plan conservative fee settings for production to avoid stalled transactions.. In practical terms, estimate costs, configure gas parameters, and use the gas reporter plugin. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas insight
keyIdea.text: Estimate in tests with the gas reporter, then plan conservative fee settings for production to avoid stalled transactions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Gas & Reporting
Architecture
Gas fields to consider
  • gasLimit — max gas units the tx can consume.
  • gasPrice — legacy gas price per unit.
  • maxFeePerGas & maxPriorityFeePerGas — EIP-1559 parameters for modern networks.
Hardhat gasReporter snippet
gasReporter: {
  enabled: process.env.REPORT_GAS !== undefined,
  currency: "USD",
  coinmarketcap: process.env.COINMARKETCAP_API_KEY,
},
Practical advice
  • Run tests with the gas reporter to estimate deployment cost.
  • Monitor provider fee suggestions and set a small buffer for production.
  • If transactions are consistently pending, raise maxPriorityFeePerGas first for speed.
Key Takeaway

Treat gas estimates as planning data and adjust fee parameters dynamically to match real network conditions.

screens.title: Using Hardhat tasks for post-deploy actions
screens.subtitle: Create and run custom tasks to attach to contracts and execute updates

narration.text: Hardhat tasks let you define reusable CLI commands that perform actions such as attaching to an existing contract and calling a function. Tasks are written in JavaScript inside the config file or a tasks folder and are registered with task(name, description). setAction. A practical use case is updating a greeting on a deployed Greeter contract without redeploying: the task accepts a contract address and the new string and then attaches via getContractFactory(). attach(address) or getContractAt. Tasks are especially useful for maintenance steps that non-developers may run, since they abstract the details of signer selection and transaction waiting. An important detail is to await tx. wait() so your task reports success only after the transaction is mined. A common misconception is that tasks replace scripts; they complement them by exposing parameterized commands that can be integrated into automation or invoked interactively. For example, you can publish a task that takes a contract address and new greeting and then run npx hardhat set-greeting --contract 0x... --newgreeting "Hello" --network sepolia. That pattern makes routine updates safer and auditable. Using Hardhat tasks for post-deploy actions means hardhat tasks let you expose parameterized, repeatable commands for contract maintenance and interactions without redeploying.. In practical terms, create and run custom tasks to attach to contracts and execute updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Automation
keyIdea.text: Hardhat tasks let you expose parameterized, repeatable commands for contract maintenance and interactions without redeploying.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Hardhat Tasks
Task example
task("set-greeting", "Sets a new greeting on the Greeter contract")
  .addParam("contract", "The Greeter contract address")
  .addParam("newgreeting", "The new greeting message")
  .setAction(async (taskArgs) => {
    const Greeter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Greeter");
    const greeter = Greeter.attach(taskArgs.contract);
    const tx = await greeter.setGreeting(taskArgs.newgreeting);
    await tx.wait();
    console.log(`Greeting set to "${taskArgs.newgreeting}" on ${taskArgs.contract}`);
  });
How to run
Invoke the task with npx hardhat set-greeting --contract 0x... --newgreeting "Hello" --network sepolia
Benefits
  • Parameterize interactions for repeatable maintenance.
  • Expose lightweight CLI for non-developers or scripts.
  • Wait for confirmations to provide deterministic success reporting.
Key Takeaway

Use tasks to encapsulate recurring post-deploy actions and reduce manual errors in maintenance steps.

screens.title: Verifying contracts and confirming addresses
screens.subtitle: Use the etherscan plugin or explorer to confirm deployed bytecode matches source

narration.text: After deployment, you should verify the contract on a block explorer so the source code and ABI are visible to users and tooling. Hardhat’s etherscan plugin uses an A P I key to submit source files and metadata for verification. In hardhat. config. js include etherscan: { apiKey: process. env. ETHERSCAN_API_KEY } and call npx hardhat verify --network sepolia. Verification ensures the on-chain bytecode corresponds to your source, which aids transparency and debugging. A practical step is to first confirm the logged deployed address matches the explorer’s transaction output. Then run the verifying command and watch the plugin submit the flattened source and compiler settings. A misconception is that verification changes the contract; it does not. It merely publishes metadata that maps source code to on-chain bytecode. If verification fails, re-check the compiler version and optimization settings in your hardhat. config. js to ensure they match what produced the deployed bytecode. Verifying gives users trust and makes ABI-driven interactions, like reading the contract from the explorer, straightforward. Verifying contracts and confirming addresses means verification publishes source-to-bytecode mapping so others can audit and interact with your deployed contract.. In practical terms, use the etherscan plugin or explorer to confirm deployed bytecode matches source. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verification
keyIdea.text: Verification publishes source-to-bytecode mapping so others can audit and interact with your deployed contract.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Contract verification
Process
Include etherscan.apiKey in config and run the verify command after deployment.
# Verify contract
npx hardhat verify --network sepolia 0xDeployedAddress "ConstructorArg1"
If verification fails, confirm the compiler version, optimisation settings, and constructor arguments match the deployed build.
Why verify?
  • Enables public inspection of source code and ABI.
  • Makes it easier for wallets and services to interact with the contract.
  • Provides transparency and trust to users.
Key Takeaway

Verification does not change on-chain state; it publishes metadata that confirms the source behind the deployed bytecode.

screens.title: Deploying an ERC-20 token to Sepolia (lab walkthrough)
screens.subtitle: Create MyToken.sol, write deployMyToken.js, fund your deployer, and verify the contract

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through deploying an ERC‑20 token to Sepolia. First, install OpenZeppelin contracts to get a secure ERC‑20 implementation. Then create a contract that mints an initial supply to the deployer inside the constructor. In the deployment script you’ll parse the initial supply using ethers. utils. parseUnits and then deploy the token with name, symbol, and supply. Before running the script, ensure your SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY are set in. env and that your deployer address has test ETH from a faucet. Execute npx hardhat run scripts/deployMyToken. js --network sepolia and watch the terminal for the deployed address and the initial minted balance. After deployment, verify the contract on a block explorer with the etherscan plugin or the manual verify command. A common misconception is to skip initial balance checks; always print the deployer balance first and confirm it has enough ETH to succeed. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › ERC-20 Deployment Lab
Contract example
// contracts/MyToken.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol";

contract MyToken is ERC20 {
    constructor(string memory name, string memory symbol, uint256 initialSupply) ERC20(name, symbol) {
        _mint(msg.sender, initialSupply);
    }
}
Deployment script
// scripts/deployMyToken.js
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();
  console.log("Deploying MyToken with the account:", deployer.address);

  const initialSupply = ethers.utils.parseUnits("1000000", 18);
  const MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyToken");
  const myToken = await MyToken.deploy("Cohortia Token", "CHT", initialSupply);
  await myToken.deployed();
  console.log("MyToken deployed to:", myToken.address);
  console.log("Initial supply minted to deployer:", (await myToken.balanceOf(deployer.address)).toString());
}

main().catch((error) => { console.error(error); process.exit(1); });
Hands-on steps
  1. Install OpenZeppelin and create the MyToken.sol contract.
  2. Configure SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY in .env.
  3. Fund your deployer from a Sepolia faucet.
  4. Run npx hardhat run scripts/deployMyToken.js --network sepolia and copy the address.
  5. Verify the contract and confirm the minted balance matches expectations.
